Reproduced at the National Archives at Seattle Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., May 16, 1919 Mrs. E. F. Briggs 4619 Woodland Park Ave. Seattle, Wash. Dear Mrs. Briggs: William has made request for vacation leave. He has been doing very well at school and I do not think it advisable to grant him leave for the full vacation period, as he will fall into habits that will cause trouble for himself and the school on re-entering next fall. During the vacation period, half the day will be given to industrial training and credit will be given him in his school work; the other half day, he may obtain work on the outside and, it may be, I shall be able to place him on the pay roll for a short time. Very respectfully, Superintendent. MMH:MC Enc. South Colby, Wash. Apr 16 - 1920 Mr. C. V. Peel Dear Sir, I just received your letter this evening saying that my son William Martin got into trouble by breaking into a store. I am grief-stricken over it. It seems as though my troubles will never be over in this world. When did he get into this trouble and when did the hearing come off, and when was he sentenced and taken to Monroe. And for how long a term is he sentenced. I will greatly appreciate a little information in regards to my boy. Thanking you in advance, I remain Sincerely, Mrs. E. F. Biggs Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 23, 1920 Mrs. E. F. Biggs South Colby, Washington Dear Madam: I have your letter of April 16 making further inquiries about your son's trouble. I sympathize with you in the burden of sorrow you feel. It appears that a number of thefts committed by some of the boys at this school were reported to the Tacoma police and that several boys were taken by the police in the early part of the year. These boys admitted the thefts and were excused on the promise to do no more stealing. But about a month ago, the owner of a store near the school, complained to the police that some of the Indian boys from this school had broken into the store and had stolen a quantity of goods. The police located the boys who admitted to the theft, and took them before the juvenile court in Tacoma. Three of the boys, one of whom was your boy, were given sentences from one to fifteen years each in the State Reform School. Your son and another boy, being over 16 years of age, were sent to Monroe, Washington. I suggest that you write your boy an encouraging letter and ask him to obey all the rules of the Reformatory and by so doing he may be able to get released in the shortest possible time. Otherwise, if he is refractory, he may be required to serve out the full sentence. I regret very much that these boys were guilty of the violation of the law, as this institution has constantly urged upon the pupils the necessity of obeying not only the rules of the school, but the laws of the State. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., April 8, 1920 Mrs. R. F. Briggs 4619 Woodland Park Ave. Seattle, Washington Dear Madam: Your son, William Martin, with some other boys, broke into a store building in the vicinity of the Cushman School and was apprehended by the police officials. After a hearing in the court, he was sentenced to serve a term at the State Industrial School at Monroe, Washington. Very respectfully, Special Agent in Charge. The law provides: "That no part of this appropriation, or any other appropriation provided for herein except appropriations made pursuant to treaties, shall be used to educate children of less than one-fourth Indian blood whose parents are citizens of the United States and of the State wherein they live and where there are adequate free-school facilities provided and the facilities of the Indian schools are needed for pupils of more than one-fourth Indian blood." (Act of August 1, 1914.) EXTRACTS FROM SCHOOL RULES. If the facilities of a school are not needed as provided in the above paragraph, children showing any Indian blood, whose parents live on an Indian reservation, and who if debarred from Government schools could not obtain an education, may be enrolled in the day and boarding schools of their reservation; these children, however, may not be transferred to nonreservation schools without special permission from the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. Before enrolling a pupil superintendents must satisfy themselves whether he has left any other school without permission and whether he has been expelled for cause from any other school. A pupil who has been expelled for cause from any Indian school may be reenrolled in any Indian school only with permission of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs. "The Secretary of the Interior may in his discretion withhold rations, clothing, and other annuities from Indian parents or guardians who refuse to or neglect to send or keep their children of proper school age in some school during a reasonable portion of each year." (27 Stat. L., 635. See 2 Dec. Comp., 308.) DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE White Earth, Minn., September 22, 1919. E. H. Hammond, Supt., Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: Replying to your letter of September 16, relative to George A. Martin, I have to advise that the blood status of George A. Martin has not yet been fixed by the Enrollment Commission, and until his status has been fixed, he will be considered as a ward of the Government. His son, William Martin, is not allotted on the White Earth Reservation. Very respectfully, [signature] Superintendent. HAA-K CASE RECORD. Respectfully, L. N. S. Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Nov. 14, 1918. Mrs. E. F. Biggs, 4619 Woodland Park Ave., Seattle, Washington. Dear Madam: In reply to your letter of the 7th instant inquiring about your son William Martin, I am pleased to advise you that he is well. The children have not written home letters this term that is quite likely the reason you have not heard from William. He no doubt has no postage nor the inclination to write. I have requested the disciplinarian to remind William of his duty to you and to write you a letter immediately. Yours very sincerely, Superintendent 4619 Woodland Park Ave. Seattle, Wash., Nov. 7, 1918. Dept. of Cushman Trades School, Dear Sir:- I have not heard from my son, William Martin, since July and would like to know what is the matter.
